#7599. St. Mary and the shrinking reach of Smith

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

Justice Clarence Thomas began Colorado’s half of the argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy with a pointed observation. In the court’s last two cases about religious schools and public benefits, Espinoza v. Montana Department of Revenue and Carson v. Makin, the justices “did not use, even cite, Smith.” So, he asked Colorado’s deputy solicitor general, “Why would we do that in this case?”

That question goes to the heart of the case. After argument, it would be surprising if Colorado won. The real fight is over how the Catholic preschools win. And the answer will determine how much is left of Employment Division v. Smith, perhaps the court’s most contested free exercise precedent.

In 2020, Colorado voters approved funding for universal preschool. The program that followed pays for 15 hours a week of preschool for every four-year-old in the state, worth about $6,300 per child. Families can spend that money at roughly 2,000 participating preschools: public, private, and religious. Every provider must accept an “equal opportunity” mandate. Specifically, children must have an equal opportunity to enroll “regardless of race, ethnicity, religious affiliation, sexual orientation, gender identity, lack of housing, income level, or disability.”

The mandate is not absolute. Colorado lets preschools use enrollment “preferences” for, among other things, children of employees, siblings, members of a specific community, and families willing to volunteer. More than 1,000 preschools use at least one. But Catholic parish preschools in the Archdiocese of Denver ask enrolling families to support the Church’s teachings on sex and marriage, and they treat children according to their biological sex. Families must affirm those teachings in good faith. Colorado says those practices violate the mandate, so the parishes cannot participate. Families who want a Catholic preschool lose the benefit. Petitioners Daniel and Lisa Sheley have lost more than $12,000 so far. The lower courts largely sided with Colorado.

The free exercise clause bars the government from “prohibiting the free exercise” of religion. For decades, the court read that guarantee to require strict scrutiny of laws that substantially burden religious practice. In 1963’s Sherbert v. Verner, South Carolina denied unemployment benefits to a Seventh-day Adventist who would not work on her Sabbath. The court held that the state could not force her to choose between her faith and a public benefit without a compelling reason.

Smith changed course in 1990. Oregon had denied unemployment benefits to two men fired for using peyote in a Native American Church ceremony. Writing for the court, Justice Antonin Scalia held that a neutral law of general applicability (that is, one that neither targets religious conduct nor exempts comparable secular conduct) needs only a rational basis, however heavily it burdens religious exercise. Under that rule, the government almost always wins.

But Smith did not overrule Sherbert. It distinguished it, and the court has spent the decades since narrowing Smith’s reach. Petitioners count eight categories of free exercise cases in which the court has declined to apply it: animus toward a religious group or person (Masterpiece Cakeshop); church autonomy (Hosanna-Tabor); discrimination among religions (Larson v. Valente); forced participation in ceremonies (Barnette); hybrid rights, which pair free exercise with another constitutional right (Cantwell); parental rights over children’s religious upbringing (Mahmoud v. Taylor); penalties on religious belief as such (McDaniel v. Paty); and the receipt of public benefits (from Sherbert through Carson). Even within Smith’s domain, a law gets strict scrutiny if it is not truly “neutral” or “generally applicable,” for example because it allows individualized exemptions (Fulton) or treats comparable secular conduct more favorably (Tandon).

The public benefits category is where Carson comes in. In three cases over five years, the court held that states may not exclude religious schools from otherwise available funding. 2017’s Trinity Lutheran involved a church preschool barred from a playground-resurfacing grant. 2020’s Espinoza involved a scholarship program closed to religious schools. And in Carson, decided in 2022, Maine paid tuition at private schools but excluded schools that taught religion. The court said all of these limits violated the free exercise clause. “Regardless of how the benefit and restriction are described,” it explained, “the program operates to identify and exclude otherwise eligible schools on the basis of their religious exercise.” Its decisions, the court said, “turned on the substance of free exercise protections, not on the presence or absence of magic words.”

The Catholic preschools offer the court two routes to strict scrutiny in this case. They track the two questions the court agreed to decide.

The first route stays inside Smith. Colorado’s mandate, petitioners argue, is not generally applicable. The state lets more than 1,000 preschools limit enrollment for secular reasons but refuses to accommodate the parishes’ religious ones. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit rejected that argument, holding that a challenger must show unfettered discretion or categorical exemptions for identical secular conduct.

The second route goes around Smith. Under Carson, the preschools argue, strict scrutiny applies whenever the government conditions a generally available benefit on giving up religious exercise, whether or not the condition is neutral. Colorado, for its part, reads Carson far more narrowly, as a rule against excluding schools because they are religious. Colorado does not exclude religious preschools as such, and many participate. On that view, Carson does not apply and Smith does.

The choice between those routes is where the real stakes lie. A win on general applicability would be narrow and fragile. It would turn on the details of Colorado’s exemptions. Colorado, or any other state, could respond by trimming its secular exemptions and excluding the same schools again. The next challenger would have to start over, hunting for a new secular comparator. Principal Deputy Solicitor General Sarah Harris called that regime “an endless sort of whack-a-mole game.”

A win under Carson, in contrast, would be far more durable. It would hold that conditioning a public benefit on abandoning religious exercise triggers strict scrutiny, however the condition is drafted. That rule would stop the kind of maneuvering Maine engaged in after Carson itself, when it rewrote its program to exclude the same religious schools without using religious labels. And it would take an entire domain, public benefits, out of Smith’s reach.

That is why Thomas’ question, which this article began with, mattered. Going in, some commentators wondered whether the court would use this case to bury Smith. CNN’s Joan Biskupic framed it that way. The argument suggested something more measured, though still significant. If the court does not overrule Smith here, it seems poised to quarantine it as far as it can.

Here’s one version of what that quarantine could look like. The court can read Carson’s public benefits rule for what it says. It can apply strict scrutiny, properly understood, in that domain. It can ground that choice in the clause’s original meaning. And it can say plainly what the United States told the court: Smith is the anomaly.

Justice Neil Gorsuch asked what Colorado’s narrow reading would leave of a decade of precedent. On Colorado’s view, he wondered, had the court been “just wasting our time for the last 10 years” on Carson,Trinity Lutheran, and Espinoza? If so, any state could escape those cases by redrafting.

Indeed, states are doing exactly that. Petitioners’ counsel, Nick Reaves, told Gorsuch that “before the ink was even dry in Carson, Maine changed its laws” so that they “don’t explicitly call out religion, but they still exclude the same families and the same schools.” Colorado’s own record shows the same pattern. The state amended its discretionary enrollment exemption process during trial. More than once, it redefined an exemption that originally allowed faith-based preschools to limit enrollment to members of their congregation. Then, while the case was on appeal, it repealed that congregation exemption entirely and argued that the repeal freed it from the district court’s injunction.

Reading Carson for what it says would not create a boundless exception. Reaves located the boundary in Smith’s own concern. Smith “was concerned about every man becoming a law unto himself,” he said, and about “broad exemptions to criminal prohibitions. That interest is not as strong when it comes to public benefits when the underlying conduct is lawful.” When Justice Amy Coney Barrett asked whether a law making the mandate a condition of every preschool’s license to operate would fall under Carson, Reaves conceded, “I don’t think that would be a Carson case.”

Harris marked a second boundary. Justice Sonia Sotomayor asked about Bowen v. Roy, a 1986 decision rejecting a Native American father’s religious objection to the government’s own use of his daughter’s Social Security number. Harris pointed to the part of Bowen that commanded a majority: “You can’t force a change in the way in which the government itself manages internal operations.” Government conduct that neither pressures nor prohibits religious exercise triggers no scrutiny, as Michalyn Steele and I have explained elsewhere about Bowen. In sum, Carson’s rule has limits on both sides. It reaches conditions on public benefits for lawful conduct, not licensing regimes or the government’s management of its own affairs.

The natural worry is what comes next. If strict scrutiny governs benefits conditions, will every program become a negotiation with every objector? Justice Elena Kagan pressed this concern. Everything, she said, would turn on whether a law passes “strict scrutiny, which is a kind of balancing test, which is like how important is the state interest? How important is the religious belief? How do we compare the one to the other?”

But that is a caricature of strict scrutiny, at least as the court applies it in this context. Gorsuch offered the more accurate account, and Harris confirmed it. “[W]e assess whether the government has a compelling interest and whether it’s narrowly tailored to that interest without balancing against the interest on the other side,” Gorsuch said. Once a claimant shows a substantial burden, “[w]e don’t go balancing the two.” Gorsuch is exactly right about that.

I do not deny that older strict scrutiny opinions sometimes used the vocabulary of balancing. But the doctrine has since been disciplined, largely through the courts’ experience with the Religious Freedom Restoration Act and the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act, passed in Smith’s wake. Courts applying RFRA and RLUIPA do not ask how central a belief is to a faith. They ask a threshold question about whether the government has objectively burdened religious exercise. At the scrutiny stage, they do not weigh the value of religion against the value of a policy. As I have argued elsewhere, strict scrutiny works as an exclusionary norm paired with a heavy evidentiary burden. It excludes all but a narrow set of permissible reasons for burdening religious exercise. Then it requires the government to prove that its action is necessary to serve one of them. That’s precisely what Gorsuch described.

The court has also adopted this disciplined approach in other contexts. In United States v. Hemani last term, it held that the government cannot disarm a person merely by naming a permissible reason. It must prove that the reason is one it actually acts on, and tie that reason to the person. As I wrote at the time, history fixed the permissible ends, and the court then demanded proof that the means served them. That is how constitutional rights work more generally: as constraints on the reasons government may act on. Strict scrutiny does not ask how much religion matters. It asks whether the state’s reason is one the Constitution permits, and whether the state can prove that reason applies to this claimant.

Harris invoked Gonzales v. O Centro, the court’s leading RFRA strict scrutiny precedent, for this very point. “I think O Centro rightly recognized strict scrutiny,” she said. “[E]ven when people say it’s tough, it is a very manageable standard for courts. It’s a familiar standard for courts.” O Centro requires the government to show that its interest is served by applying the law “to the person,” meaning “the particular claimant whose sincere exercise of religion is being substantially burdened.” Courts must look “beyond broadly formulated interests” to the harm of granting the specific exemption requested.

The track record bears this out. Gorsuch noted that the federal government “already has to meet strict scrutiny” in providing its many public benefits. Harris pointed to the federal experience under RFRA and to “the 40 states that have RFRA equivalents.” Under the pre-Smith regime, she added, cases “turned out both ways.” Public schools already operate under this regime. The District of Columbia’s schools are subject to federal RFRA. As Gorsuch put it, Senators Ted Kennedy and Orrin Hatch “would be quite surprised to think that RFRA created laws unto themselves in every American.”

Smith, by contrast, is the unstable regime. The court’s cases have left what Harris called “a mess,” in which “it’s hard to describe Smith as a default, and it’s even harder to describe Smith as a workable default in this particular context.” Strict scrutiny is the familiar standard. Smith, in her words, is “a much less stable jurisprudence.”

Restoring strict scrutiny for benefits conditions would also move free exercise doctrine closer to the clause’s original meaning. Two justices asked whether strict scrutiny is faithful to that meaning, and both counsel answered yes.

Barrett asked Reaves whether strict scrutiny is “what you think is required by the original meaning.” Reaves answered that Sherbert v. Verner is “much closer to the original meaning than Smith.” He pointed to the “peace and safety provisos” in founding-era state constitutions, which protected religious exercise unless it threatened public peace or safety. Barrett then put the point precisely: “So you see it as an implementing doctrine that’s close to how it would have been implemented at the time of the founding?” “I think that’s right, yes,” Reaves said. Gorsuch asked Harris a parallel question. Is strict scrutiny, as the court announced it in Sherbert and Thomas v. Review Board and applied it in the recent benefits cases, “a reasonable construction of … the original meaning?” Harris said yes.

That framing is right. Strict scrutiny is not itself the original meaning. It is a doctrine for implementing that meaning, a form of what originalists call constitutional construction. Mark Storslee and I made this argument in our amicus brief in the case, which petitioners’ counsel also cited at argument for the history of Catholic exclusion from the common schools. The brief draws on my work elsewhere, including Constructing Constitutional Rights and Replacing Smith.

The core of the argument is this. The founding generation did not let religious exercise yield to any reason government happened to articulate. Early state constitutions took some justifications for burdening religious exercise off the table. Others, most commonly the protection of public peace and safety, were permissible. And founding-era courts made the government show that it was actually advancing one of those permissible interests before religious exercise had to give way. For example, in People v. Philips, decided in 1813, a New York court refused to force a Catholic priest to testify about a confession. Compelling him, the court explained, would place him “between Scylla and Charybdis,” and the priest’s silence posed no threat to the peace or safety the state constitution protected. That is what strict scrutiny requires: a permissible reason, proven on the facts.

The evidence from Reconstruction points the same way. The 14th Amendment, which applies the free exercise clause to the states, was framed by a generation shaped by religious resistance to the Fugitive Slave Act. Abolitionist believers insisted on a right to give a fugitive shelter and a “crust of bread,” whatever neutral and generally applicable law said. As Kurt Lash and I have explained, that understanding informed the amendment’s privileges or immunities clause. Judge Ryan Nelson of the 9th Circuit relied on that history in a recent concurrence concluding that Smith “breaks from the history and tradition surrounding free exercise and the Fourteenth Amendment.” At argument, Harris agreed with Justice Brett Kavanaugh that, as a matter of original meaning and contrary to Smith, the free exercise clause is “more than simply a protection against explicit discrimination.”

One serious question about the Carson approach came from Kavanaugh. A rule that applies strict scrutiny to benefits conditions, but not to outright bans, would impose “greater First Amendment scrutiny on a benefits program than … an outright ban on the religious conduct.” That, he said, “seems inverted.” On petitioners’ theory, a state that merely withholds funding would face strict scrutiny, while a state that banned the same conduct outright, through a neutral law, would get only Smith’s rational basis review. He acknowledged one answer, that the court “should just overrule Smith entirely,” but asked Reaves to assume that was off the table.

The incoherence is real. And if the court doesn’t overrule Smith in this case, hopefully it will take that step someday soon. But the incoherence belongs to Smith itself. Harris put it directly: “Smith is the anomaly in the context of public benefits or in any other context, where other rights do not have this so long as a law is generally applicable rational basis review.”

Smith itself claimed the opposite, calling religious exemptions “a constitutional anomaly.” As Mark Rienzi and I have argued, the reverse is true. Exemptions are a species of as-applied challenge, the default remedy elsewhere in constitutional law. The anomaly is Smith’s rule, not the exemptions it disfavors.

The court has retired other precedents it no longer believes in. It distinguishes them, whittles them away, and finally overrules them. Teague v. Lane’s “watershed” exception for new rules of criminal procedure went unused for 32 years before Edwards v. Vannoy declared it “moribund” and eliminated it. Gorsuch joined that opinion. Abood v. Detroit Board of Education was cabined inHarris v. Quinn before Janus v. AFSCME overruled it. Lemon v. Kurtzman was sidestepped for years before Kennedy v. Bremerton confirmed that the court had “long ago abandoned” it.

After decades of whittling, quarantine is the penultimate stage of that life cycle. The court can further limit Smith’s damage now. Eventually the court will likely complete the life cycle and retire Smith altogether.

The most striking moments in the argument were strict scrutiny questions in all but name. Justice Samuel Alito asked how many times the feared harm had actually happened, and observed that there was “little evidence of a practical problem.” Barrett asked whether there was any record of LGBTQ parents being turned away from these preschools, and whether any entity other than religious ones had sought an exemption from the mandate. “No, Your Honor,” Colorado’s counsel answered. Kavanaugh asked the state, “Why not seek the win/win?” With roughly 2,000 preschools in the program and 34 Catholic ones, he saw “plenty of opportunities to respect the rights of the religious believers and respect the ability of LGBT parents to find” a school that fits. “Why has this been provoked?” he asked.

Those are the questions narrow tailoring forces a government to answer. Strict scrutiny asks whether the state can prove that its reason applies here, not merely name it. That demand makes room for the win-win Kavanaugh described. Religious preschools can serve the families who want them, and every family can find a school that fits. Smith invites the opposite: winner-take-all conflicts provoked by a rule that never asks whether the conflict was necessary.

The best case for quarantining Smith is not that religious claimants deserve to win. It is that strict scrutiny asks the questions this argument kept asking: Why are we here, and couldn’t we have avoided this conflict? A rule that makes the government answer those questions is easy to administer. It is also faithful to the clause’s original meaning.

Disclosure: The author was amicus curiae in support of the petitioners in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy.

Stephanie Barclay is a Professor of Law at Georgetown Law School, and the Faculty Director of the Georgetown Center for the Constitution.

#7598. Georgia is back at No. 1 in AP Top 25 ahead of Utah and Notre Dame; Ohio State drops to No. 21

UGA turned in one of the most dominant performances of the season.

Georgia was voted No. 1 in The Associated Press Top 25 for the second time this season Sunday, unbeaten UCLA matched its highest ranking in 25 years and Ohio State’s free fall continued after a wild weekend that followed the first College Football Playoff rankings of the year.

Miami became the fourth No. 1 team to get knocked out of the top spot, the most in a single season since 2008. Only one team â No. 6 Indiana, which was idle â remained in the same spot it had a week ago in the Top 25.

Georgia turned in one of the most dominant performances of the season in a 42-7 victory at Mississippi on Saturday. The Bulldogs had been No. 1 for one week when they were upset by Auburn on Oct. 17 but never dropped out of the top five, and they were the voters’ choice for No. 1 by a wide margin over Utah and Notre Dame.

Utah moved up one spot to No. 2 after its 28-20 win over rival BYU and the Utes now have their highest-ever AP ranking in the regular season. The Fighting Irish’s 31-24 win over Miami pushed them up one rung to No. 3, while the Hurricanes fell to No. 5 after their first loss.

Georgia earned 53 of the 70 first-place votes from the media voting panel. Utah received 12 first-place votes and Notre Dame got five.

UCLA is 9-0 for the first time since 1998 and moved up to No. 4. It’s the Bruins’ highest ranking since their 2001 team was No. 4 following a 6-0 start. After Miami, Indiana, Alabama, Texas, Tennessee and Texas Tech completed the top 10.

Alabama and Texas both were rewarded for road wins and moved up two spots. The Crimson Tide won at LSU and the Longhorns at Missouri.

Tennessee jumped from No. 16 to No. 9, its highest ranking in two years, after an impressive 34-6 win over a top-10 Kentucky. Texas Tech returned to the top 10 after outscoring West Virginia 53-48.

Ohio State, which was No. 2 two weeks ago, went from No. 11 after its loss at Southern California to No. 21 this week after a 41-28 home loss to Oregon. The Buckeyes hadn’t been ranked so low, excluding the 2020 pandemic season, since 2014.

#7597. Russell Brand found guilty of rape, sexual assault as judge promises ‘sentence of some length’

British comedian, actor and podcaster Russell Brand arrives at the Southwark Crown Court in London on the fourth day of his trial on charges of rape, sexual assault and indecent assault. Brand pleaded not guilty to all charges. (Photo from Shutterstock)

Actor and comedian Russell Brand was found guilty in London on Thursday of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others.

The four-week trial, which happened in the Southwark Crown Court in London, examined seven charges brought by six women from 1999 to 2009.

Brand, 51, initially faced three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of indecent assault. He was convicted of four encounters, including a 2004 sexual assault involving grabbing a woman’s breasts in London’s Soho district and the rape of another woman inside his home in 2009.

High Court of England and Wales Judge Joel Bennathan rejected Brand’s bail application, remanded him to custody and told him to expect “a custodial sentence of some length,” according to coverage by Courthouse News Service.

Brand is expected to be sentenced Monday. He denied the charges during his four-hour testimony, saying the sexual encounters were consensual. He is also being investigated for additional rape allegations made by two other women.

#7596. Democrats plan to push clean energy to lower bills and challenge Trump’s fossil fuel agenda

Democrats can begin investigations and hold hearings into climate policy rollbacks and elimination of green energy grants by the Republican administration, potentially trying to undo some changes and restore renewable energy incentives.

Some Democrats are promising to push for more clean energy to help tackle rising energy costs when they take control of Congress in January, though President Donald Trump says he will use his veto power aggressively.

With new majorities in the House and Senate after last week’s midterms, Democrats can set an agenda boosting clean energy and addressing climate change. While those are traditionally core priorities of the party, climate was not a central topic in this election cycle.

Democrats can begin investigations and hold hearings into climate policy rollbacks and elimination of green energy grants by the Republican administration, potentially trying to undo some changes and restore renewable energy incentives.

Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, the top Democrat on the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works, said Trump’s clean energy attacks drove up prices for taxpayers. He said Democrats will “work every angle to lower consumers’ energy costs, and we will demand accountability for the massive corruption wrought by Trump’s fossil-fuel donors.”

American Clean Power Association CEO Jason Grumet said everybody who is trying to build clean energy “feels bolstered.”

Enacting major changes would require Republican support because Democrats will lack the numbers to override presidential vetoes. Even then, lower energy bills are not guaranteed because prices also depend on fuel costs, demand and the expense of maintaining the electric grid.

“The wins give Democrats more leverage over spending and more political power to advance a coherent agenda; the question is whether they’ll use that power effectively,” said Lisa Sachs, director of the Columbia Center on Sustainable Investment. “The vote was for affordability and opportunity. Democrats now need to be clear about which policies deliver them.”

Trump said after Tuesday’s election that Democrats will send over “things that are insane” and he will veto them, speaking generally about legislation. But in the comments to Fox News, he predicted that “after a couple of months of vetoes,” he and Democrats will find ways to work together.

The White House said in a statement Wednesday that Trump is “committed to unleashing reliable, affordable, and secure energy sources to lower prices, strengthen our grid, and protect our national security, and is willing to work with anyone to accomplish this.”

Trump promised to lower energy prices. Instead, his war with Iran and other policies increased the price of gasoline, diesel and electricity. At the same time, the administration canceled many clean energy projects and grants and slowed clean energy permitting.

Trump particularly dislikes offshore wind. Developer Orsted said Thursday that Revolution Wind, a large wind farm in federal waters off Rhode Island, has started operating commercially.

Will the president change his tune on green energy? That’s doubtful, said former Sen. Byron Dorgan, D-N.D., co-chair of the government relations practice at ArentFox Schiff.

“He is likely to keep pushing his energy issues, and I think he will be forced to give some room for a new Congress to recreate a different strategy that will add clean energy,” Dorgan said in an email.

Trump promotes expanding production of oil, natural gas and coal, which cause climate change, because he argues that would give the U.S. the lowest-cost electricity. Mike Sommers, CEO of the American Petroleum Institute, the oil and gas industry’s top lobbying group, said that as voters have changed the balance of political power in Washington, “the affordability message is unmistakable.”

Sommers said in a statement there is a real opportunity for bipartisan cooperation to reduce costs and strengthen the economy, starting with an energy permitting reform proposal announced in September. The legislation is aimed at shortening the timeline to get big energy projects started.

Ife Kilimanjaro, executive director of the U.S. Climate Action Network, said Democrats should reject that proposal and use their stronger position to pass legislation that actually builds out much-needed clean energy.

The administration has reshaped the Environmental Protection Agency, reversing pollution limits as it promotes fossil fuels.

Clear Street energy transition analyst Tim Moore said he expects Democrats to investigate the climate and environmental rollbacks, in an effort to block some from taking effect. Democrats could also try amending the Clean Air Act to cut carbon pollution and push back against EPA budget cuts, he added.

Rep. Sean Casten, D-Ill., said he is cautiously optimistic some Republicans will now seek to differentiate themselves from Trump and back pro-environmental policies. But without Republican support, Democrats’ more ambitious bills will largely lay out their agenda for 2028, he added.

Climate is not necessarily at the top of Democrats’ list of priorities. They are targeting healthcare access, trade tariffs and the Iran war.

Rep. Frank Pallone, the New Jersey Democrat who is expected to become chair of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, said the party should focus on healthcare, affordability, consumer and environmental protections, clean energy and regulating Big Tech.

David Victor, a professor of innovation and public policy at the University of California, San Diego, largely expects a stalemate at the federal level on climate and energy policy because of the divided government. He said agreement could come on some bipartisan measures such as a permitting overhaul.

Victor thinks Democratic-led investigations and hearings will center on corruption and other topics that may only touch on energy and climate. Like Casten, Victor said many of the Democratic bills likely will not become law, but will outline what Democrats could accomplish if they win the White House in 2028.

“The Democrats are going to be drafting things that the administration’s not going to like. They don’t have the votes to override a veto, and on top of it, the administration is going to be in turmoil because of its own electoral failures and because of all the investigations,” Victor said. “This seems to me, at the federal level, largely a recipe for kind of intense chaos over the next two years.”

One of the biggest wild cards is the behavior of the administration, which could use executive power to double down on rollbacks of climate and environmental rules, he said.

Democrats scored victories in races for governor in states long controlled by Republicans, including Texas and Georgia.

Leah Stokes, a political scientist at the UC Santa Barbara, said there could be a lot of state action on climate next year because of those wins. That is where climate leadership has traditionally come from, she noted. At the federal level, Stokes is optimistic about extending clean energy tax credits since some Republicans support that.

Jay Inslee, a former Democratic governor and congressman from Washington, also expects growing momentum for clean energy in states that elected Democratic governors, particularly in states where they also won legislative majorities.

“This is a really powerful instrument for the United States to join the rest of the world and get back in a leadership position, even if we still have a climate denier that might exercise a veto on some things that we want to do federally,” Inslee said. “So I hope people will pay attention to the big progress we’re going to make on a state-level basis.“By JENNIFER McDERMOTT Associated Press

#7595. Court leans toward narrow ruling on inmate’s use of habeas for accelerated transfer to a halfway house or home confinement

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court heard oral argument on Nov. 2 in Maxwell v. Dinis about whether a federal inmate may use a habeas statute, 28 U.S.C. § 2241, to contest the Federal Bureau of Prisons’ refusal to accelerate his transfer to a halfway house or home confinement.

Maxwell, a former attorney, was convicted at trial for his role in conspiring with a mob-related organization, La Costa Nostra, to take over a Texas-based mortgage-loan company, FirstPlus Financial Group, Inc., and drain it of its assets. As Maxwell neared the end of his sentence, he sought to contest the BOP’s calculation of good-time credits that would accelerate his transfer from prison to a halfway house or home confinement. The question for the court was whether Section 2241, which does not clearly spell out what claims may be brought but whose scope has largely been shaped by precedent, allows him to do so.

Maxwell’s attorney, Masha Hansford, pressed for a broad rule that habeas is available to an inmate like Maxwell who is asserting a right to a “distinct and lower level of custody.” But that position almost immediately encountered some pushback. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson questioned “whether we really need to use this case to define every circumstance in which habeas is appropriate.” Hansford agreed that the court need not adopt a test that allows inmates to challenge all changes to the level of custody and was content to have the court resolve Maxwell’s case by applying a narrower test endorsed by the government that would permit an inmate to use habeas to challenge the denial of an accelerated transfer to parole or, as here, a halfway house or home confinement.

Justice Samuel Alito pressed Hansford on whether an inmate may use Section 2241 simply to dispute how BOP calculated good-time credits or whether the inmate must also show that any error in calculating would also entitle the inmate to accelerated transfer to a halfway house or home confinement. After Hansford replied that Maxwell met all the requirements for the transfer and only the calculation of good-time credits was at issue, Justice Neal Gorsuch followed up by pressing whether the court needs to say that an inmate could bring a habeas challenge about the calculation of good-time credits alone. Hansford replied that the court did not need to say a dispute over good-time credits alone would suffice for a federal inmate to bring a claim in Section 2241.

Turning to Hansford’s level-of-custody test, Justice Sonia Sotomayor noted that, in a prior case, Justice Antonin Scalia had referred to habeas as covering a “‘quantum change’ in the level of custody,” but Hansford was asking the court “to create new language, ‘materially less restrictive custody.’ Why don’t we stick to what we have?” Hansford agreed that the court need not broaden its test and that Maxwell’s requested transfer to a halfway house or home confinement amounted to such a quantum change.

Assistant to the Solicitor General Kevin J. Barber, arguing for the government, contended that “there’s no need to adopt” Maxwell’s “amorphous level-of-custody rule.” He explained that the court “has always made clear that habeas is available when your claim is seeking discharge from actual physical confinement in prison to a different kind of custody,” such as a halfway house or home confinement. Here, the government relied heavily on Preiser v. Rodriguez, which held that habeas supplies the sole avenue for a state inmate to challenge the denial of credit toward release on parole.

When Gorsuch pressed Barber on the source of the government’s rule and why an inmate’s transfer to solitary confinement or maximum security would not be covered, Barber pointed principally to history and tradition in the court’s habeas cases. Barber explained, “we don’t have any tradition of claims being recognized as habeas claims challenging just transfers within prison systems.”

Despite agreeing that Maxwell could bring his claim in Section 2241, the government argued that no court could actually grant him relief. Specifically, the government pointed to 18 U.S.C. § 3621(b) and its terms barring courts from reviewing “a designation of a place of imprisonment under this subsection.” According to the government, service of a sentence in a halfway house or home confinement is “a designation of a place of imprisonment” governed by that statute.

But the government did not appear to have the votes to prevail on this argument, at least at the Supreme Court. Justice Brett Kavanaugh pressed Barber on whether that issue could be left for the lower court to decide on remand. Barber conceded that the court “absolutely could.” Sotomayor questioned Barber about whether the government is right that Section 3621(b) applies to Maxwell’s claim. But after Barber began responding, Justice Amy Coney Barrett reiterated Kavanaugh’s point that “we don’t have to get into any of this, right?” Barber again agreed.

Jackson pressed Barber on a separate point, that the BOP is expected to transfer Maxwell to a halfway house or home confinement in January 2027, which would soon make his claim moot. Jackson disputed why the court would revisit its decision to hear the case. Barber apologized for not pressing the Section 3621(b) issue or mootness in opposing certiorari, but said these factors spoke in favor of the court dismissing the case as improvidently granted.

The amicus, Brian W. Barnes, was appointed to argue in favor of the ruling by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit that habeas is unavailable for Maxwell’s claim. When pressed by Justice Elena Kagan, Barnes agreed that habeas is available to “encompass a move from incarceration to parole,” as Preiser held. Kagan pointed out that “parole looks an awful lot like what’s going on here.”

The justices’ questions suggest that they are unlikely to limit Preiser and reject an analogy between Maxwell’s requested relief and the parole in that case. The justices also showed little appetite for reaching the government’s Section 3621(b) argument. How they would handle Maxwell’s expected release to a halfway house in January 2027 was less clear, but that circumstance could result in a speedier ruling.

Richard D. Cooke worked for the U.S. Department of Justice for 23 years, first at the Antitrust Division for 5 years and then as an Assistant United States Attorney in the Eastern District of Virginia for 18 years.

#7592. Congress returns to a changed Washington after GOP election wipeout

The halls of the Capitol are expected to swell this week with the collision of incoming and outgoing lawmakers, as the newcomers attend orientation sessions while the retiring lawmakers start to clear out.

WASHINGTON (AP) â Congress returns Monday to a changed Washington, the Democrats having trounced Republicans in the midterm elections, but with President Donald Trump doubling down on his political threats despite the landmark GOP losses.

Newly elected lawmakers arrived on Capitol Hill over the weekend, creating a jumble of split-screen moments reflective of the new political landscape. Dozens of jubilant Democrats, families and suitcases in tow for freshman orientation, appeared emboldened by the party’s sweep of power. The trickle of Republicans coming in spoke soberly of the GOP’s vast challenges ahead.

âThis country sent a clear message from coast to coast, and that message is theyâve had enough of whatâs gone on," said Rep.-elect Daniel Biss, D-Ill. “Theyâve had enough of Donald Trump. Theyâve had enough of MAGA. And critically, they are ready to transform who holds power, and what they do with it.â

Republican Rep.-elect Chris Stigall of Missouri said it’s clear that voters sent a loud message, “and I hope, as a new member, I can be on the ground level of figuring out how we can reconnect.â

For starters, he said, the GOP needs to understand that the economy is not where it needs to be. âSix-dollar diesel, I will tell you, for the farmers in my district, that is a tough pill to swallow.â

But first, it’s out with the old before the new Congress takes over in January.

The House and Senate are in session for just six short weeks of a lame-duck sprint to finish up the Republican agenda before the GOP majorities come to an end, making way for the change of power on Jan. 3, 2027.

Leadership elections and a government funding package are all priorities ahead.

One first order of business is expected to be a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over his leadership at the Pentagon.

Republican Rep. Thomas Massie pushed the impeachment resolution forward over the objections of House GOP leadership as momentum grows to hold Hegseth accountable for the Iran war, which many Republicans blame for the party’s midterm election wipeout.

House Speaker Mike Johnson had tried to prevent a vote on Hegsethâs impeachment in September and abruptly halted proceedings by sending lawmakers home early.

But itâs unclear Johnson, who remains close to Trump, will be able to slow the drive for impeachment now, unless he decides to adjourn the chamber again.

Trump defended Hegseth to reporters on Sunday night before he flew back to Washington after spending the weekend at his Florida home.

âHeâs guilty of two things, basically winning two wars,â Trump said. âI believe we saved the Middle East and Israel combined. And itâs awfully hard to say letâs impeach somebody who did that.â

Democrats are expected to widely support the impeachment resolution and a number of Republicans have signaled they could join them.

âIâm a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution,â House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said Sunday on ABC.

Jeffries said it’s time for Hegseth to go, and that the secretary âhas abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran."

The halls of the Capitol are expected to swell this week with the collision of incoming and outgoing lawmakers, as the newcomers attend orientation sessions while the retiring lawmakers start to clear out.

At the same time, Trump has tapped top aide Stephen Miller, the hard-right architect of much of the White Houseâs domestic policy agenda, as his new chief of staff. Miller takes the helm Monday in what is expected to be the start of a more direct confrontation with the Congress.

Republicans in both the House and Senate are planning to hold their leadership elections this week in closed-door meetings that could end up being blame-casting sessions about what went wrong in the elections.

House Republicans are bracing for a contentious leadership battle after Johnson decided to step aside, setting up a showdown between the No. 2 Republican, Rep. Steve Scalise of Louisiana, and Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio, the brawling former wrestling coach allied with the hard-right conservatives.

The two men had confronted one another when trying to become House speaker three years ago, but neither was able to win enough support from the Republican rank and file, leading to Johnson’s rise. With the House Republican numbers now shrunken, lawmakers could seek wholesale change in leadership.

In the Senate, Majority Leader John Thune is expected to retain his job as Republican leader, though in the minority as Democrats flipped Republican-held seats, including milestone wins in Texas and Kansas.

Democrats are expected to hold their elections later this month. At least two Democrats â Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton of Kansas â have declined to publicly support Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer’s bid to be the majority leader, but no challenger for the job has emerged.

âI think we need somebody whoâs going to bring us together and somebody whoâs going to – somebody whoâs going to come with fresh ideas to what weâre doing,â Hamilton said Sunday on CNN.

Jeffries, who is on track to make history as the nation’s first Black speaker of the House, faces skepticism from voices in the party’s left wing.

âEvery single member here is going to have their individual vote,â said Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, chairman of the Congressional Progressive Caucus at a Capitol press conference Sunday, flanked by newly elected lawmakers, including a handful from the Democratic Socialists of America.

âWhat we talked about at orientation today was not about any individual person, but about policy,â Casar said. âHow we set a progressive path forward.â

The Republican majority had high hopes for a legislative run to secure party priorities in the final weeks of the session, but those plans now seem doubtful.

Congress still needs to fund the government by mid-December or risk another federal shutdown if the money lapses.

It also hopes to pass the annual defense bill, which sets policy for the Pentagon and delivers pay-raises for the troops, and has been approved by Congress essentially every year since World War II. But this year, the defense package is tangled over progressive pressure to cut money for the Iran war and military aid to Israel over the war on Gaza.

The Senate hopes Monday to launch votes on legislation to speed permitting reviews for new energy infrastructure projects. Trump in a social media post Sunday pushed senators to act.

And there is pressure on the Senate to swiftly confirm Trump’s judicial nominees before Republicans lose control of the chamber in January.

#7591. Justices grapple with how to apply pretrial procedure rules in improper firing dispute

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

How rigidly to apply the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure surfaced this week in Younge v. Fulton Judicial Circuit District Attorney’s Office, Georgia, argued on Nov. 2, in which the Supreme Court addressed whether a defendant’s failure to amend its pleading and present an affirmative defense prevents that party from moving for summary judgment on the basis of that defense. To put it perhaps a bit too simply, a number of justices made clear that rules exist for a reason and should be followed.

As detailed in my preview of the case, the pretrial procedural issues arise in the context of a civil rights suit in which the plaintiff asserts that she was improperly dismissed from her job. Jasmine Younge held a high-level position in the Fulton County District Attorney’s Office for about two months until she was fired in July 2019 by District Attorney Paul Howard. Younge says she was dismissed from her job about two weeks after telling Howard that she was pregnant. Subsequently, she sued the Fulton County District Attorney’s Office for a number of civil rights violations, including the claim that she was terminated because of her pregnancy in violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

The DA’s office answered the complaint but never asserted in its pleadings the personal-staff exemption defense upon which it prevailed at summary judgment. (Under Title VII, certain officials are exempted from the statutory definition of employee, including members of an elected official’s “personal staff.”) Younge objected unsuccessfully to the motion, arguing as a procedural matter that it had been too late for the DA’s office to assert new affirmative defenses given that it had not amended its pleading.

Younge based her argument on Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 16(b)(4), which requires the district court to issue a pretrial scheduling order that may be modified only upon a showing of “good cause.” The pretrial scheduling order sets deadlines for the parties and, as relevant here, limits the time for parties to amend their pleadings.

Younge’s objection also was supported by Rule 15(a)(2), which sets out the standard for a litigant to amend a pleading. Under the 1962 case of Foman v. Davis, still the leading Supreme Court case on amendment under Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 15(a), the court is required to consider a number of factors, including “undue delay, bad faith or dilatory motive on the part of the movant, repeated failure to cure deficiencies by amendments previously allowed, [and] undue prejudice to the opposing party by virtue of allowance of the amendment.”

The lower courts, including the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit, analyzed only whether Younge would be prejudiced by allowing the personal-staff defense to be asserted. They found that there was no prejudice and concluded on the merits that Younge was a member of the district attorney’s personal staff and therefore not covered by Title VII.

Younge successfully petitioned for review of the 11th Circuit’s judgment regarding whether amendment is required before a defendant may move for summary judgment on the basis of an unpled affirmative defense.

Eric Schnapper, an experienced Supreme Court advocate, argued on behalf of Younge at the Supreme Court. The initial questions from Justices Clarence Thomas and Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson focused on prejudice. That seems to be because even if, as Younge argued, the DA’s office did not follow Rule 15(a)(2) and amend its pleading before moving for summary judgment, the question remained: Why did the failure to amend matter when “undue prejudice” was a factor to be considered under Foman and the 11th Circuit found that Younge was not prejudiced by the DA’s failure to amend?

Yet Justice Amy Coney Barrett homed in on the core point of Younge’s argument when she stated, “going back and forth about whether you were prejudiced or not doesn't help you in your fundamental argument, which is that, procedurally, this wasn't done right.”

After several follow-up questions from Justice Elena Kagan, Schnapper responded by adopting a modest but clear position: “[T]he Court should reverse this decision, send it back, and tell the defendant if it wants to raise [an] affirmative defense to move to amend. That’s all we’re asking this Court to hold.” Over the course of the argument, his approach seemed to grow in its appeal to the justices.

Barrett also asked whether the defendant would have to file a separate motion to amend its answer or the court effectively could “construe” the defendant’s summary judgment motion as a motion to amend. She noted that the 10th Circuit has such a rule in which the court applies the standards for whether amendment is allowed without requiring the defendant to “go through the formalist exercise of actually filing a Rule 15 or 16 motion” to amend.

Schnapper did not reject the approach suggested by Barrett, commenting, “You would have to be sure to let the parties brief” whether amendment was proper. To be sure, Schnapper did not endorse the 10th Circuit’s approach. But so long as the district court is required to be asked for leave to amend, whether in a separate motion to amend or as part of a summary judgment motion, Younge would prevail in the Supreme Court because the DA’s office never sought amendment.

Several justices questioned the need for reversal and remand given the 11th Circuit’s finding that Younge had not shown prejudice by the DA office’s failure to bring this defense in its pleadings. Thomas asked what prejudice Younge suffered, commenting at one point, “I thought it was admitted that she was a member of his personal staff.” Justice Samuel Alito also seemed to resist the requirement of “a formalistic rule about filing a motion to amend for an affirmative defense.”

Stephen Petrany argued on behalf of the Fulton County DA’s office. During his argument, several justices expressed discomfort about adopting the 11th Circuit’s prejudice standard without requiring amendment. Justice Neil Gorsuch inquired about an “incredibly dilatory” affirmative defense, such as one asserted “because of reasons of bad faith,” and why that would be acceptable.

When Petrany replied that the court “has the inherent authority” to reject a summary judgment motion on that basis, Gorusch said “[t]hat seems to be an admission that Rule 15 … applies,” requiring a request to file an amended pleading so that the court can consider the conduct of the party moving for summary judgment (which may have been dilatory) as well as the actual or claimed prejudice on the nonmoving party. Shortly after that exchange, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson expressed her concern that Petrany’s position would “disincentivize parties to actually bring motions to amend.”

The court’s order granting certiorari included a question about Rule 16(b)(4), which provides that the pretrial schedule “may be modified only for good cause and with the judge's consent.” In this case, because the DA’s office moved for summary judgment after the discovery period had closed (which would have been after the deadline in the pretrial schedule for amending pleadings had passed), Younge argued that Rule 16(b)(4) applies in addition to Rule 15(a)(2), which generally governs amendment of the pleadings.

There were a number of questions about Rule 16(b)(4) during the argument, including whether it was necessary to consider this rule in order to decide the case. But the court seems likely to land where Kagan did during an exchange with Petrany: To reverse and remand the 11th Circuit with instructions to require the DA’s office to amend its answer to include the personal-staff defense and for the lower court to determine whether to allow that amendment under Rule 15(a)(2) and the factors in Foman.

Of course, it may be the case that the lower courts will allow the amendment and that the DA’s office will again prevail on its summary judgment motion. But, even if they would not have changed the ultimate outcome in this case, as Kagan put it, “The rules provide standards here. Why not just use them?” A majority of the justices seemed to agree.

Rodger D. Citron is the Associate Dean for Research and Scholarship and Professor of Law at Touro University, Jacob D. Fuchsberg Law Center.

#7590. Over $157 million in pro bono legal services donated by law class of 2026

The Class of 2026 has donated more than $157 million in pro bono work, or more than 4.3 million hours in legal services, according to an Association of American Law Schools released Friday.

That’s an average of 197 of donated hours per student, according to this fall’s survey of 110 law schools which reported on 22,249 students, or about 58% of the class of 2026 in ABA-accredited schools. With a value of $36.14 an hour, according to nonprofit coalition Independent Sector, the donated time has an estimated value of $157 million.

And these numbers might be low, according to the report, since the hours are difficult to track and did not include law students in master’s degree programs. Total donated hours could be more than $250 million if average hours per student were applied to the total enrollment of all AALS member law schools, the study states.

In the decade since the survey was established, it has reported more than $1 billion in legal services contributions from law students.

Many law schools now emphasize serving clients in legal deserts. Some offer remote pro bono opportunities and others offer clinics, externships and fellowships. For instance, University of Nebraska College of Law Rural Estate Planning Clinic, law students provide free estate‑planning services to senior citizens in rural communities, preparing documents like wills, powers of attorney, living wills and transfer‑on‑death deeds.

“Access to justice is a first principle for legal education and the legal profession,” Danielle M. Conway, AALS president, said in the release. “The pro bono and clinical legal work done by today’s law students help to bridge access to justice gaps and reinforce the profession’s obligation to serve every community.”

#7588. DOJ steps up its investigation into the Dobbs leak

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

This week, during the first half of the November argument session, the justices heard oral arguments in four cases and quickly declined a request from the Trump administration to intervene in a voting dispute in California. However, headlines about these developments were overshadowed by Tuesday’s midterm elections. The blue wave brought new significance to debates over court reform and when Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas might retire.

Today, the justices will meet in a private conference to discuss cases and vote on petitions for review. Orders from today’s conference are expected on Monday at 9:30 a.m. EST.

On Thursday, the Supreme Court denied two requests for a stay of execution from Jesse Guardado, who was sentenced to death for the 2004 murder of Jackie Malone. Hours later, Guardado was executed in Florida.

On Wednesday, the justices heard argument in Guerrero v. Johnson, on the limited circumstances in which a state prisoner can return to federal court for a second round of post-conviction review. Here is the link to our Case Preview.

On Tuesday, the justices heard argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, a religious discrimination challenge brought by Catholic preschools in Colorado over the state’s requirement that all schools participating in its universal preschool program must admit everyone – including LGBTQ children and children with LGBTQ parents. Here are the links to our Case Preview and Argument Analysis.

On Monday, the justices heard argument in Maxwell v. Dinis, on a federal inmate’s ability to use a habeas statute, 28 U.S.C. § 2241, to contest the Federal Bureau of Prisons’ refusal to accelerate his transfer to a halfway house or home confinement. Here are the links to our Case Preview and Argument Analysis.

The justices also heard argument on Monday in Younge v. Fulton Judicial Circuit District Attorney’s Office, Georgia, on whether an affirmative defense may be asserted as a basis for summary judgment if not presented earlier in a pleading. Here are the links to our Case Preview and Argument Analysis.

Monday morning, the Trump administration returned to the Supreme Court’s interim docket, asking the justices to intervene in its efforts to keep California from counting ballots cast by individuals who it contends are noncitizens. Just hours later, the court denied the request. There were no noted dissents.

Later on Monday, the court released its calendar for the January argument session, which will begin on Monday, Jan. 11.

On Oct. 21, the Trump administration asked the court to allow it to resume construction of its border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas. The request has been fully briefed since last Friday, and the court’s decision could come at any time.

Looking ahead, the justices will hear arguments on Monday in two cases: Nielsen v. Watanabe, on whether and when federal officials can be held liable for constitutional violations; and Hoffmann v. WBI Energy Transmission, Inc., on whether the “just compensation” paid to land owners losing property to a pipeline project should be determined by referring to state law, which often provides for a higher payment than what the Constitution requires.

Jodi Kantor and Michael S. Schmidt, The New York Times

In May 2022, Politico released a leaked draft of the Supreme Court’s decision in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, which overturned the right to abortion. The leak was “a seismic breach of confidentiality” and led to “an internal inquiry by the court,” although “no leaker has ever been publicly identified.” But The New York Times reported on Thursday that the Justice Department is now “pursuing a criminal investigation into who leaked” the draft opinion and that this “investigation has ramped up in recent weeks as prosecutors have sent grand jury subpoenas for testimony and sought information from people who worked at the court at the time of the leaks.”

On Thursday, defenders of “a Cook County, Illinois, ordinance that makes it unlawful to sell or possess any ‘assault weapon or large capacity magazine,’ including AR-15 rifles,” asked the Supreme Court to dismiss a challenge to the ban that’s set to be argued in December, Viramontes v. Cook County. Attorneys for Cook County contended that the case is now moot after the “lead plaintiff, Cutberto Viramontes, asked [on Oct. 29] to be removed from the litigation without explanation.” Although the filings represent “a puzzling twist” in the case, “whether Viramontes is permitted to withdraw would have limited practical significance for the broad question of whether state and local governments may ban AR-15-style rifles,” according to CNN. That’s because Viramontes was consolidated with another case on a similar law in Connecticut, “which would continue even if the Supreme Court decided to dismiss the Cook County litigation. And whatever the court decides on Connecticut’s ban would almost certainly affect whether other bans like the one in Cook County can stand.”

Tuesday’s midterm elections “all but guaranteed” President Donald Trump won’t be able to put a fourth justice on the Supreme Court. Beginning in January, Democrats will have “a Senate majority—with a several-seat cushion—that will make it easy to block Trump judicial nominees, especially for any Supreme Court vacancies that might arise in 2027 or 2028,” according to The Wall Street Journal. Faced with this reality, “[s]ome legal observers have floated a last-ditch scenario in which [Clarence] Thomas or [Samuel] Alito could announce their retirement in the coming days and give Trump and the outgoing Republican Senate a chance to quickly install a successor before the newly elected Congress is seated on Jan. 3.” But the Journal described this scenario as “exceedingly unlikely,” in large part because neither Alito nor Thomas appears interested in retiring. And it’s not “clear that a Supreme Court nominee could get through the lame-duck Congress even if there were a retirement, especially because some moderate Republican senators are on their way out of office and blame Trump for losing their seats.”

In a Thursday interview with the Associated Press, Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said “that Democrats will not allow President Donald Trump to put ‘a right-winger’ on the Supreme Court once they take power.” He “would not say if he would hold a Supreme Court vacancy open until after the next presidential election, as former Senate Republican leader Mitch McConnell did in 2016. But he said that Democrats are ‘not going to allow any crappy nominees’ to be confirmed to the Supreme Court.” “The bottom line is we’re not going to allow a right-winger on the court,” Schumer said.

In a column for Bloomberg, Noah Feldman contended that Tuesday’s election results “should cause Democrats to reconsider the wisdom of plans to pack the court or strip it of jurisdiction over certain issues.” It should no longer feel as urgent to make such changes, according to Feldman, because “[i]f a Democrat wins the presidency in 2028 and the Democrats hold the Senate, the Democrats will have a chance to flip the court from 6-3 conservative to 5-4 liberal” simply by filling predicted or expected vacancies. The reform proposals floated in recent months “make little sense if Democrats take seriously the prospect of a liberal recapture of the institution,” Feldman wrote.

The Supreme Court heard argument on Monday in Maxwell v. Dinis on whether a federal inmate may use a habeas statute to contest the Federal Bureau of Prisons’ refusal to accelerate his transfer to a halfway house or home confinement.

The argument on Nov. 10 in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards brings the justices a complex constitutional problem: Does the Constitution allow Congress to delegate to the executive branch – as opposed to the courts – the authority to adjudicate the obligation of an employer to comply with employment agreements it makes with temporary immigrant workers?

In his Empirical SCOTUS column, Adam Feldman offered an in-depth analysis of Justice Elena Kagan, examining not only how she votes, but also how she chooses to agree and disagree.

In her Ratio Decidendi column, Stephanie Barclay revisited Tuesday’s argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, noting that the discussion put a spotlight on 1990’s Employment Division v. Smith, a controversial ruling that made it easier for the government to overcome free exercise challenges. The ruling in St. Mary, according to Barclay, “will determine how much is left of” Smith, which has already fallen out of favor with the court.

In his Relist Watch column on Wednesday, John Elwood explored four petitions for review that will get a second look from the justices at today’s conference. Three concern a long-running dispute over Alabama’s congressional districts and the fourth asks whether using a car makes an otherwise local kidnapping a federal crime – even when the car never crosses a state line.

In his Courtly Observations column on Tuesday, Erwin Chemerinsky explored Nielsen v. Watanabe, in which the court is considering under what circumstances federal officers may be sued for money damages for constitutional violations, noting that the case comes at a time when efforts “to hold ICE agents accountable” have taken on new urgency.

On Oct. 19, the Supreme Court granted review in Association for Education Fairness v. Montgomery County Board of Education, a case on race and school admissions. In his AV Ristorante column on Monday, Brian Fitzpatrick explained why he believes “it could be the final nail in affirmative action’s coffin.”

Sarah Isgur and David French discuss the Texas Supreme Court’s blue wave, the possibility of a majority-Democrat Supreme Court, and one of the biggest Supreme Court cases of the term: St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy.

Friday’s A Closer Look is typically a judicial biography. This week we cover Justice Peter V. Daniel, who served on the court from 1841/2 to 1860.

Like some of the other justices we’ve covered, Justice Peter V. Daniel is one that “[f]ew recall or have ever heard of.” Those who know of Daniel have not been complimentary. He has been called “a brooding proslavery fanatic” according to law professor Earl Maltz, and a 1965 book review likened him to the notoriously bigoted Justice James C. McReynolds, minus McReynolds’ occasional “charm.”

Daniel was born in April 1784 on his family’s estate in Stafford County, Virginia. After studying with private tutors and a brief stint at the College of New Jersey (now Princeton University), he read law in Richmond under Edmund Randolph, President George Washington’s attorney general and secretary of state. In 1810, Daniel married Randolph’s daughter, Lucy.

In November 1808, Daniel fought a duel in Maryland against businessman John Seddon; Seddon later died from his injuries. This did not appear to significantly slow Daniel’s career, however: He subsequently spent two one-year terms in the Virginia House of Delegates, a tenure his biographer, John P. Frank, judged as “utterly undistinguished.” In 1812, Daniel joined Virginia’s Council of State, which advised the governor, and from 1818 to 1835 served as lieutenant governor. His “friends” “apparently lacked any real warmth or affection for him, complaining of his ‘frozen deportment,’” which played out literally: In the winter of 1813, Daniel reportedly balked at spending a modest sum to keep militiamen warm, despite their officer’s warning that the men’s lives were at stake, on the reasoning that Virginia state law made the soldiers responsible for their own clothing.

Daniel’s Richmond law practice was modestly successful, but he had other aspirations. Through the Richmond Junto (a Virginia Democratic-Republican network) he organized and led the state’s Jacksonians, and, along with then-New York governor Martin Van Buren, built an “Albany-Richmond axis,” which backed Andrew Jackson for president. Daniel subsequently turned down Jackson’s offer of attorney general. In 1836, however, he accepted a federal judgeship in eastern Virginia, Jackson’s reward for his party loyalty and his support for the president’s war on the national bank.

When Justice Philip Barbour died in February 1841, Van Buren had roughly a week left in office and rushed to nominate Daniel to the court. Aware of Daniel’s reputation, Whig senators tried to stall the vote, at one point walking out together to leave the chamber without a quorum, while Democratic leaders searched the capital for their own absent senators. Daniel was ultimately confirmed 22-5 in a midnight vote. The exact date he took the oath is unclear; the Federal Judicial Center lists it in January 1842 “based on questionable authority,” while one biography entry has him joining the court in December 1841.

After he joined the bench, Daniel’s circuit assignment included Arkansas and Mississippi, which involved arduous trips from Washington. While circuit riding in 1851, for example, Daniel rode in a canal boat for two days to get from D.C. to Pittsburgh (and was not a fan of the other “vulgar and filthy” passengers).

On the court itself, close to one in three of Daniel’s written opinions was a dissent, and during his tenure, his solo dissents outnumbered any other justice’s by more than two to one. He fought against extending federal admiralty power to inland waters, and when the court did just that in 1852’s Genesee Chief v. Fitzhugh, Daniel was the lone dissenter. Perhaps his best-known majority opinion came in 1848’s West River Bridge Co. v. Dix, which put Daniel opposite the famed lawyer and statesman Daniel Webster. Daniel detested Webster so much that, after meeting him, he reported his hand “was actually contaminated by contact with his.” In the case, Vermont had taken over a privately chartered toll bridge, paid compensation, and opened it as a free road, but the bridge company argued that the takeover breached the contract clause of the Constitution. Writing for the majority, Daniel held that the franchise was ordinary property that the state could take through eminent domain.

Daniel, who was a slaveholder, concurred in 1842’s Prigg v. Pennsylvania, which held that the federal Fugitive Slave Act preempted Pennsylvania’s ban on recapturing formerly enslaved persons. After Van Buren joined the antislavery Free Soilers, Daniel’s friendship with him ended, and Daniel reportedly swore he would never again set foot north of Maryland (he came to blame even bad weather on the North). In Dred Scott v. Sandford, Daniel argued that freed slaves could not be citizens because they had once been held as property and that the Northwest Ordinance of 1787 (which, among many other things, had kept slavery out of land north and west of the Ohio River) was unconstitutional, thus taking a more extreme position than even Chief Justice Roger Taney, who wrote the majority opinion.

Daniel’s first wife, Lucy, died in 1847, and his second wife died in 1857 after a candle accidentally lit her clothes on fire. Daniel died in Richmond in May 1860 following a lengthy illness. In February 1861, Republican senators blocked President James Buchanan’s pick to replace him, Jeremiah Black, making the seat one of the three vacancies that President Abraham Lincoln filled in 1862. It stayed open until July 1862, when Lincoln chose Justice Samuel Miller.

In a December 1860 memorial, the attorney general said that Daniel “held the pen of a ready writer,” but “was sometimes in danger of going too directly to his purpose and treating with too much contempt the obstacles that intervened.”

JUSTICE THOMAS: “Does Atkins ever stop being a new rule?”

MR. SCHEPERS: “In our view, Atkins was new at the time it was decided.”

JUSTICE THOMAS: “We're talking about now, though.”

MR. SCHEPERS: “That – we believe that Atkins was new based off of the character of the decision in 2002 and that it remains new now.”

JUSTICE THOMAS: “What about Marbury v. Madison?”

#7586. Democrats won control of Congress. So what does that mean for the Supreme Court?

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

Democrats won big in Tuesday’s midterm elections, flipping at least 40 seats in the House and at least seven in the Senate. Come January, the Democratic Party will control both houses of Congress, which will allow it to set policymaking priorities and play a lead role in shaping the future of the Supreme Court.

Most immediately, the power shift in the Senate will complicate (if not effectively eliminate) President Donald Trump’s ability to appoint another justice to the Supreme Court, should a vacancy arise after the new Congress is seated. The Democratic Party will have enough votes to reject a nomination – if it even allows confirmation hearings to proceed.

Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.

#7585. Legal sector jobs hit record high in October, new data shows

Data from the U.S. Department of Labor shows that employment in the U.S. legal sector hit a record high in October. (Image from Shutterstock)

Legal sector jobs have reached a record high, hitting more than 1.25 million positions for the first time in October, according to seasonally adjusted data released by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics on Friday.

Last month, 1,251,200 people worked in lawyer, paralegal and other law-related professional roles, up 2,400 jobs from September and 3,200 jobs from August, according to Law360, which reported on the government statistics.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics also notes that jobs in the legal sector have increased each month since March, Law360 reports. They have grown by 22,800 year over year.

The broader economy in the United States added 165,000 jobs in October, according to Reuters, which has additional reporting. The unemployment rate fell to 4.1% last month.
